title: Jaishankar Says the U.S. Asked India to Buy Russian Oil. Then It Imposed Tariffs.
excerpt: At Finland’s Kultaranta Talks, India’s foreign minister laid out the receipts: Washington needed Indian refiners to stabilise crude markets in 2022. Now it is taxing them.
body:
Jaishankar Just Said What Indian Diplomats Usually Only Think. Washington Asked India to Buy Russian Oil. Then It Imposed Tariffs.

External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar dropped his sharpest public critique of U.S. trade policy to date at the Kultaranta Talks in Finland on Thursday, revealing that Washington explicitly asked India to buy Russian crude oil in 2022 to stabilise global energy markets — and then punished it with tariffs for doing exactly that.

“At that time, the US specifically asked India to buy Russian oil to stabilise the oil market,” Jaishankar told the audience at the presidential retreat near Turku, participating in a session on ‘Emerging Powers and the New Geopolitical Competition.’

The comments came just hours before he called U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to protest the killing of three Indian sailors in American strikes near the Strait of Hormuz — a sharp week in the India-U.S. relationship by any measure.

## The Oil Play, Reconstructed

Jaishankar laid out the sequence with unusual clarity. When Western sanctions hit Russia after the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, European nations abruptly pivoted away from Russian energy and scrambled to lock in supplies from the Middle East — India’s traditional source. That sudden European demand surge threatened to spike global oil prices beyond what importing nations could bear.



> **"“At that point of time, much of the oil available in the market was from Russia because Europeans were buying up the Middle East oil, which was our traditional supplier,” Jaishankar explained."**


Washington’s solution was pragmatic: ask India to absorb the Russian crude that Europe was no longer buying. India obliged, sharply increasing its purchases of discounted Russian oil. Indian refiners processed it, resold products on global markets, and helped prevent a catastrophic price spiral.

“At that point of time, much of the oil available in the market was from Russia because Europeans were buying up the Middle East oil, which was our traditional supplier,” Jaishankar explained. “Circumstances pushed us in a certain direction.”

The result was a win for global markets, a win for Indian refiners, and — for a while — a win for Washington’s inflation management. India’s Russian oil purchases rose from under 2% of its crude imports pre-2022 to roughly 40% by 2025.

## Then Came the Tariffs

But the gratitude did not last. The Trump administration has proposed an additional 12.5% tariff on imports from India and several other countries, alleging the use of forced labour — a charge India has rejected. Separate reciprocal tariffs already in place have strained bilateral trade, which both sides are now trying to stabilise through a phased trade agreement.

India’s Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said last week that the first tranche of a deal could be concluded by mid-July. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer is expected to visit India the week after the G7 summit to push negotiations forward.

Jaishankar’s comments at Kultaranta were carefully calibrated — they didn’t name Trump, didn’t use inflammatory language, and stuck to a factual reconstruction of events. But the message was unmistakable: India did what it was asked to do, and it expects the favour to be remembered, not repaid with trade barriers.

## The Timing Is Not Accidental

The Kultaranta remarks came at a geopolitically charged moment. Jaishankar was in Helsinki en route to Nice, where Prime Minister Modi has arrived for bilateral talks with French President Macron and the Bharat Innovates deep-tech showcase. From Nice, Modi will proceed to the G7 summit at Évian, where a bilateral with Trump on Wednesday will cover trade, visas, energy, and the Hormuz crisis.

The sailor deaths and the oil tariffs now sit side by side on the agenda. India is walking into the G7 meeting with more leverage — and more grievances — than it has had in years.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs in the United States, the trade tension matters directly. A breakdown in negotiations could affect H-1B processing goodwill, tariff exemptions on Indian goods, and the broader diplomatic climate that underpins business ties between the two countries. Indian professionals in tech, finance, and manufacturing operate within an ecosystem that depends on stable trade relations.

Jaishankar’s Finland comments also speak to a deeper strategic calculation. India is signalling that it will not be a transactional partner that absorbs requests from Washington without reciprocity. For a diaspora that often finds itself navigating between two national identities, the calibration of that message — firm, factual, unburnt — will matter as much as the message itself.

The G7 bilateral on Wednesday will reveal whether Washington heard it.
